title: Scientific English for Researchers
text:
Preface
English is the main language of international research. For most researchers in the world it is a second (or third) language, and writing, reviewing and presenting in it takes extra time and effort. Amano et al. (2023) surveyed researchers in environmental sciences from many countries and found that non-native speakers spend substantially more time reading, writing and preparing presentations in English, and are more likely to have papers rejected or sent back for revision because of the language. This is a structural inequality of the research system, not a personal failing. This book cannot remove it, but it can make the work faster and the results clearer.
It is written for doctoral students and researchers in any field, with particular attention to the difficulties of Spanish speakers. It does not teach general English: it focuses on the genres researchers need (articles, abstracts, reviews, cover letters, emails, talks) and on the evidence about what makes scientific texts clear.

title: Scientific English for Researchers
text:
Map of the book

6. Presenting and networking

Each chapter has objectives, a glossary, a required reading with a DOI, labs that run in your browser, activities with instant feedback, an assignment and a self-assessment. The Phrasebank collects useful expressions for every section of a paper. Your progress is saved only in your browser.






TipA note on AI tools



Language tools and AI assistants can help you edit, but they can also introduce errors, change your meaning or invent references. Use them as an editor, not as an author: check every change, keep your own voice, and follow the journal’s policy on disclosing their use.

title: Chapter 1. The architecture of a research article
text:
1. One paper, one message
Mensh & Kording (2017) start with the most important rule: focus your paper on a single central contribution, which you can state in the title. Everything else serves that message. If you cannot write it in one sentence, the paper is not ready to be written.
They also recommend writing for the naive human reader: someone intelligent but outside your sub-field, who reads quickly and remembers little. Short sentences, defined terms and a logical flow help experts too.
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1. The architecture of a research article

title: Chapter 1. The architecture of a research article
text:
2. IMRaD








Section
Question it answers
Typical verb tense




Introduction
Why does this matter, what is unknown, what did you do?
Present (known facts), past (previous studies), present (aim)


Methods
How exactly did you do it?
Past, often passive or “we”


Results
What did you find?
Past


Discussion
What does it mean, how does it fit, what are the limits?
Present for interpretation, past for your findings



Mensh and Kording suggest a context-content-conclusion scheme at every level: the paper, each section and each paragraph start by giving context, present the content and end with a conclusion. The first sentence of a paragraph should announce its message; the last should close it.






Figure 1: The hourglass shape of a research article: broad context, a narrow question and methods, and a widening discussion.
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1. The architecture of a research article

title: Chapter 1. The architecture of a research article
text:
3. The introduction: Swales’s CARS model
John Swales’s analysis of introductions, the CARS model (Create a Research Space), describes three rhetorical moves:

Establish a territory: show that the topic is important and summarise what is known.
Establish a niche: show a gap, a problem, a contradiction or an unanswered question.
Occupy the niche: state your aim, what you did and (often) what you found.

Example:

Doctoral attrition rates exceed 30% in many countries (territory). However, most studies rely on cross-sectional surveys, and little is known about how supervision changes over time (niche). Here, we followed 1,200 doctoral students for five years to examine… (occupy).
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1. The architecture of a research article

title: Chapter 1. The architecture of a research article
text:
4. The abstract
Many journals ask for a structured abstract (Background, Methods, Results, Conclusions). Even when they do not, a good abstract follows the same moves in 150-250 words: context and gap, aim, methods, main results with numbers, and the main conclusion. Avoid references, undefined abbreviations and vague promises such as “results are discussed”.
crumbs: 1  Chapter 1. The architecture of a research article

title: Chapter 1. The architecture of a research article
text:
Worked example






NoteFrom a vague abstract to a structured one



Before: “This paper studies doctoral supervision. Data were collected and analysed. Several interesting results were found, which are discussed in relation to the literature.”
After: > Background: About one in three doctoral students leave before completing. Aim: We examined whether supervision quality predicts completion better than funding. Methods: We followed 1,200 doctoral students at 14 Spanish universities for five years. Results: Students reporting high-quality supervision were half as likely to drop out (hazard ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.40–0.65); funding had a smaller effect. Conclusions: Doctoral programmes should invest in supervisor training as well as funding.
The second version states the gap, the method, numbers and a conclusion a reader can act on.

Basic. Which CARS move is missing from this introduction: “Open data is important. Here, we survey 500 researchers about their data-sharing practices.”?

title: Chapter 2. Clear sentences
text: Plavén-Sigray, P.; Matheson, G. J.; Schiffler, B. C.; Thompson, W. H. (2017). The readability of scientific texts is decreasing over time. eLife, 6, e27725.

title: Chapter 2. Clear sentences
section: 1. Scientific texts are getting harder to read
text:
1. Scientific texts are getting harder to read
Plavén-Sigray et al. (2017) analysed more than 700,000 abstracts from biomedical and life-science journals published between 1881 and 2015. Readability, measured with standard formulas, decreased steadily, partly because of more general scientific jargon (“robust”, “underlying”, “novel”) and longer sentences. Hard-to-read texts reduce the reach and the reproducibility of research: a method that cannot be understood cannot be repeated.

title: Chapter 2. Clear sentences
text:
2. Readers’ expectations
Gopen and Swan’s classic advice on scientific writing can be summarised in a few principles:

Subject and verb close together and early. Readers wait for the verb; a long subject delays understanding.
Topic position (the beginning of a sentence) holds old information that links to what came before.
Stress position (the end of the sentence) holds the new, important information.
One main idea per sentence. Long sentences are not wrong; long sentences that hide the action are.


Hard: The determination of the extent to which open data mandates were associated with increases in data reuse across disciplines was the aim of this study.
Clear: We examined whether open data mandates increased data reuse across disciplines.

title: Chapter 2. Clear sentences
text:
3. Three habits that cloud sentences








Habit
Example
Better




Nominalisation (verbs turned into nouns: -tion, -ment, -ance)
We performed an analysis of the data.
We analysed the data.


Unnecessary passive
It was found by the authors that…
We found that…


Wordy phrases
due to the fact that; in order to; a large number of
because; to; many



The passive is not forbidden: it is useful when the agent is unknown or irrelevant (Samples were stored at −80 °C). Many journals now encourage we for the authors’ actions.

title: Chapter 2. Clear sentences
Chapter 2. Clear sentences
text:
Worked example






NoteEditing a paragraph step by step



Original (52 words): “The implementation of an evaluation of the effectiveness of the mentoring programme was carried out by the research team, and it was found that there was a significant reduction in the level of anxiety of the participants due to the fact that they had access to regular meetings.”

Find the real action: evaluate. Make it a verb with a subject: We evaluated…
Replace wordy phrases: due to the fact that → because.
Turn nominalisations into verbs: a reduction in the level of anxiety → anxiety fell.
Put new information at the end: …because they met their mentors regularly.

Edited (20 words): “We evaluated the mentoring programme and found that participants’ anxiety fell significantly, probably because they met their mentors regularly.”

title: Chapter 2. Clear sentences
text:
Graded exercises
Basic. Rewrite: “An increase in the number of citations was observed.”

Show solution
“Citations increased.” or, with an agent, “We observed that citations increased.”

Advanced. Edit a paragraph of your own writing with the four steps of the case and compare the readability scores before and after in the lab.

Show solution
Report the word count and the score before and after, and explain each change. Check that no technical precision was lost.

title: Chapter 3. Hedging and stance
text: Required reading

title: Chapter 3. Hedging and stance
text: Hyland, K. (1996). Writing without conviction? Hedging in science research articles. Applied Linguistics, 17(4), 433-454.

title: Chapter 3. Hedging and stance
text:
1. Why researchers hedge
Hyland (1996) analysed hedging in research articles in cell and molecular biology and showed that it is not a sign of weakness but a central feature of scientific argument. Hedges (may, might, suggest, possibly, appear to, likely) do two jobs: they state claims accurately, matching them to the evidence, and they show respect for the reader and the community, leaving room for disagreement. Boosters (clearly, demonstrate, undoubtedly, it is well known that) do the opposite: they express certainty.
Good scientific writing calibrates: strong evidence, strong verbs; weak or indirect evidence, cautious verbs.








Strength
Verbs and expressions
Use when




Strong
show, demonstrate, establish, confirm
Robust, replicated evidence, ideally causal


Moderate
indicate, suggest, support
Good evidence with limits (observational, single study)


Tentative
may, might, could, possibly, it is possible that
Speculation, interpretation, future directions

title: Chapter 3. Hedging and stance
text:
2. Overclaiming and spin
Overclaiming (saying more than the data allow) is common in abstracts and press releases: causal language for correlational data (“X causes Y” instead of “X is associated with Y”), generalising from a sample to a population, or calling a non-significant result “a trend towards significance”. Reviewers and readers notice, and it damages credibility.
But excessive hedging is also a problem, especially for non-native writers who learn that caution is safe: “It might possibly be suggested that the results could perhaps indicate…” says nothing. One hedge per claim is usually enough.

title: Chapter 3. Hedging and stance
text:
3. Reporting other people’s work
Reporting verbs carry your stance towards a source:

Neutral: Smith (2020) reports / describes / finds that…
Positive: Smith (2020) shows / demonstrates / establishes that… (you accept the claim)
Critical or distant: Smith (2020) claims / asserts / argues that… (you leave room for doubt)

title: Chapter 3. Hedging and stance
Chapter 3. Hedging and stance
text:
Worked example






NoteCalibrating a discussion paragraph



Original: “Our results prove that mentoring causes better completion rates and clearly demonstrate that all universities must implement mentoring programmes.”
Evidence: one observational cohort study in one country.
Calibrated: “Our results suggest that mentoring is associated with higher completion rates. Because the study was observational, we cannot rule out that more motivated students sought mentors. If confirmed in experimental studies, these findings would support investing in mentoring programmes.”
Changes: prove → suggest; causes → is associated with; the alternative explanation is stated; the recommendation becomes conditional.

title: Chapter 3. Hedging and stance
text:
Graded exercises
Basic. Replace the booster in: “This method undoubtedly outperforms all previous approaches.”

Show solution
For example: “In our tests, this method outperformed the three approaches we compared it with.” It states the evidence instead of asserting certainty.

Advanced. Take the conclusions of a paper in your field and rewrite them so that each claim matches the strength of its evidence.

Show solution
Identify the design of each piece of evidence (experimental, observational, replicated) and choose verbs accordingly; add limitations where the evidence is indirect.

title: Chapter 4. Common errors and false friends
text:
2. Uncountable nouns
These nouns have no plural and do not take a/an: research, evidence, information, equipment, software, feedback, advice, knowledge, progress, work (in the sense of effort). Data is plural in traditional usage (these data are) but often singular today (this data is); be consistent and follow the journal.

✗ several researches → ✓ several studies / much research
✗ an evidence → ✓ a piece of evidence / some evidence
✗ softwares → ✓ software packages / tools

title: Chapter 4. Common errors and false friends
text:
4. Academic vocabulary
1 compiled the Academic Word List (AWL): 570 word families that are frequent across academic disciplines but not in general English (analyse, approach, assess, concept, data, establish, factor, interpret, method, significant…). Together they made up around 10% of the words in her corpus of academic texts. Learning them, with their typical collocations (conduct a study, draw a conclusion, raise a question, address a gap), pays off more than learning rare technical terms.

title: Chapter 4. Common errors and false friends
text:
Worked example






NoteCorrecting a paragraph by a Spanish speaker



Original: “Actually, the researches about this topic are scarce. In this work we have realised an study with 1.250 students, which consisted in a survey. The informations obtained depend of the faculty.”
Corrected: “Research on this topic is currently scarce. In this study, we conducted a survey of 1,250 students. The information obtained depends on the faculty.”
Errors fixed: actually (false friend) → currently; researches (uncountable) → research; realised (false friend) → conducted; an study → a study; 1.250 → 1,250; consisted in → (restructured); informations → information; depend of → depends on.

text: Noble, W. S. (2017). Ten simple rules for writing a response to reviewers. PLOS Computational Biology, 13(10), e1005730.
crumbs: 5  Chapter 5. Peer review and correspondence

title: Chapter 5. Peer review and correspondence
text:
1. Cover letters
A cover letter to an editor is short (one page) and answers three questions: what you are submitting, why it matters to this journal’s readers, and formal statements (originality, no simultaneous submission, conflicts of interest, data availability). Do not repeat the abstract.

Dear Dr Smith,
Please find attached our manuscript “Supervision quality predicts doctoral completion: a five-year cohort study”, which we submit for consideration as a Research Article in Higher Education.
Most studies of doctoral attrition are cross-sectional. Following 1,200 students for five years, we show that changes in supervision quality predict completion better than funding. These findings will interest readers working on doctoral education policy.
The manuscript has not been published or submitted elsewhere. All authors approved it and declare no conflicts of interest. Data and code are available at [DOI].
Yours sincerely,
crumbs: 5  Chapter 5. Peer review and correspondence

title: Chapter 5. Peer review and correspondence
text:
2. Writing a review
A useful review has a clear structure: a summary of the paper’s claims (to show you understood them), the main concerns (validity, methods, interpretation), minor points, and, if the journal asks, a recommendation. Be specific (“the model does not control for cohort; please add it or explain why not”) and kind: criticise the work, not the authors. Avoid asking for a different paper.
crumbs: 5  Chapter 5. Peer review and correspondence

title: Chapter 5. Peer review and correspondence
text:
3. Responding to reviewers
Noble (2017) offers rules that turn a stressful task into a manageable one. The most important:

Provide an overview, then respond to every point, quoting each comment in full.
Be polite and respectful to all reviewers, even when they are wrong.
Accept the blame when the reviewer misunderstood: it usually means the text was unclear, so clarify it.
Make the response self-contained: the editor should not need to search the manuscript; quote the changed text.
Respond to the reviewer’s intent, not only the literal request.
Be clear about what changed, with page and line numbers.
When you disagree, give evidence and reasons, and consider doing the requested analysis anyway (perhaps in the supplement).








Instead of
Write




The reviewer is wrong.
We respectfully disagree, because…


This was already explained.
We have clarified this point in the Methods (p. 6, lines 120-128).


We do not have time to do this.
This analysis is beyond the scope of this study, but we now mention it as a limitation (p. 15).
crumbs: 5  Chapter 5. Peer review and correspondence

title: Chapter 5. Peer review and correspondence
text:
4. Academic emails
Short, with a clear subject line and the request in the first two sentences. Formal openings (Dear Professor García,), a polite request (Would you be able to…? I would be grateful if…) and a closing (Best regards, / Kind regards,). Avoid Spanish calques such as I write you to… (→ I am writing to…) and Waiting for your answer (→ I look forward to hearing from you).
crumbs: 5  Chapter 5. Peer review and correspondence

title: Chapter 5. Peer review and correspondence
text:
Worked example






NoteAnswering three reviewer comments



Comment 1: “The sample is not representative.” → We agree that the sample is not representative of all doctoral students. We now describe its composition in detail (p. 6) and have restricted our conclusions to public universities (p. 18).
Comment 2: “Please add a reference to Smith (2019).” → We thank the reviewer. We have added this reference and discuss how our results compare (p. 15, lines 320-326).
Comment 3: “The authors should use a multilevel model.” → We agree that the data are nested. We have re-run the analysis with a multilevel model (students within universities). The results are very similar (Table S3), and we report them in the supplement.
Each response: thanks or acknowledgement, what was done, where.

title: Chapter 6. Presenting and networking

title: Chapter 6. Presenting and networking
section: 1. Speaking at conferences as a non-native speaker
text:
1. Speaking at conferences as a non-native speaker
Amano et al. (2023) found that non-native English speakers reported spending more time preparing oral presentations and that many avoided attending or presenting at international conferences because of language. Knowing this is useful in two ways: preparation pays off, and the difficulty is shared by most of your audience. International audiences value clarity far more than a native accent.

title: Chapter 6. Presenting and networking
text:
2. Signposting
Signposting language tells the audience where they are in the talk. It is even more important in a second language, for you and for listeners.







Function
Phrases




Opening
Today I’m going to talk about… / The question I want to address is…


Outline
First, I’ll… Then… Finally…


Moving on
Let’s move on to… / That brings me to…


Pointing to a visual
As you can see in this graph… / The key thing here is…


Emphasising
What’s really important is… / I’d like to stress that…


Concluding
To sum up… / The main take-home message is…


Inviting questions
I’d be happy to take any questions.

title: Chapter 6. Presenting and networking
text:
3. Pronunciation that matters
Intelligibility depends more on word stress and sentence stress than on individual sounds. Common problems for Spanish speakers:

Word stress in academic words: anaLYsis, ANalyse, deVELop, DAta or DAHta, preSENT (verb) vs PREsent (noun), PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy.
Initial s + consonant: study, Spain, specific (not estudy).
Final consonants and -ed endings: analysed (/d/), tested (/ɪd/), worked (/t/).

Mark the stress in your script, record yourself and listen.

title: Chapter 6. Presenting and networking
text:
4. Questions and discussion

Ask for clarification: Sorry, could you repeat the question? / Do you mean…?
Buy time: That’s a good question. Let me think…
Admit limits: I’m not sure, but my guess would be… / That’s beyond the scope of this study, but…
Redirect politely: That’s an interesting point; perhaps we could discuss it after the session.

title: Chapter 6. Presenting and networking
text:
5. Networking
Prepare a 30-second elevator pitch: who you are, what you study and why it matters, in plain words. Ask questions about the other person’s work, follow up by email within a week, and remember that coffee breaks are where many collaborations start.

title: Chapter 6. Presenting and networking
text:
Worked example






NoteScript and signposting for a five-minute talk



Opening: “Imagine starting a PhD with 1,200 other students. Five years later, one in three has left. Today I’d like to show you why.”
Outline: “First, I’ll explain how we followed these students. Then I’ll show what predicted who stayed. Finally, I’ll suggest what programmes can do.”
Transitions: “So that’s how we collected the data. Let’s move on to what we found.” / “This brings me to the main result.”
Conclusion: “To sum up: supervision matters more than money. The main take-home message is that programmes should train supervisors.”
Questions: “Thank you. I’d be happy to take any questions.”

title: Chapter 6. Presenting and networking
text:
Graded exercises
Basic. Choose the right phrase to move from methods to results.

Show solution
For example: “Let’s move on to the results.” or “So what did we find?”

Advanced. Write the full signposted script of a five-minute talk on your research, mark the stressed syllables of ten key words and record yourself.

Show solution
Check that every section has an explicit transition, that the main message is stated at the start and at the end, and compare the recording with the script for stress and pace.

title: Appendix C — Teacher’s guide
text:
Suggested assessment
The book can be used as the textbook of a doctoral workshop of about 18-24 hours (six sessions) on scientific English, or for self-study. It assumes an intermediate level of English (around B2) and focuses on research genres rather than general English.
The common rubric values structure and argument (25%), clarity and concision (25%), accuracy of language (20%), appropriate academic style (20%) and reflection (10%).

title: Appendix D — Glossary
text:
The architecture of a research article
Terms in the book, by chapter.

title: Appendix D — Glossary
text:
IMRaD
Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion: the standard structure of research articles. → Chapter 1


Rhetorical move
A unit of text with a specific communicative purpose, such as showing a gap. → Chapter 1


CARS model
Swales’s Create a Research Space model of introductions: territory, niche, occupation. → Chapter 1


Research gap
What is not yet known or resolved, which the study addresses. → Chapter 1


Structured abstract
An abstract with labelled parts: background, methods, results and conclusions. → Chapter 1


Context-content-conclusion
Scheme for papers, sections and paragraphs recommended by Mensh & Kording (2017). → Chapter 1

title: Appendix D — Glossary
text:
Clear sentences

Readability
How easy a text is to read, often estimated with formulas such as Flesch Reading Ease. → Chapter 2


Topic position
The beginning of a sentence, which should hold old, linking information. → Chapter 2


Stress position
The end of a sentence, which should hold new, important information. → Chapter 2


Nominalisation
A verb or adjective turned into a noun (analyse → analysis), often making sentences heavier. → Chapter 2


Passive voice
Construction in which the subject receives the action (samples were stored). → Chapter 2


Plain language
Clear, direct writing that the intended reader can understand on first reading. → Chapter 2

title: Appendix D — Glossary
text:
Hedging and stance

Hedge
Word or phrase that softens a claim (may, suggest, possibly). → Chapter 3


Booster
Word or phrase that strengthens a claim (clearly, demonstrate). → Chapter 3


Stance
The writer’s attitude towards claims and sources. → Chapter 3


Overclaiming
Stating more than the evidence supports, for example causal claims from correlations. → Chapter 3


Reporting verb
Verb used to report sources (show, suggest, claim), which conveys stance. → Chapter 3

title: Appendix D — Glossary
text:
Common errors

False friend
Word that looks similar in two languages but has a different meaning. → Chapter 4


Uncountable noun
Noun with no plural form (research, evidence, information). → Chapter 4


Academic Word List
Coxhead’s list of 570 word families frequent across academic disciplines. → Chapter 4


Collocation
Words that habitually go together (conduct a study, draw a conclusion). → Chapter 4


Calque
Literal translation of an expression from another language (make a research). → Chapter 4

title: Appendix D — Glossary
text:
Peer review and correspondence

Cover letter
Short letter to the editor that accompanies a submission. → Chapter 5


Response to reviewers
Document that answers each reviewer comment and explains the changes. → Chapter 5


Major and minor revision
Editorial decisions asking for substantial or small changes before acceptance. → Chapter 5


Politeness strategies
Linguistic choices that soften requests and criticism. → Chapter 5


Rebuttal
Reasoned disagreement with a reviewer’s comment, supported by evidence. → Chapter 5

title: Appendix D — Glossary
text:
Presenting and networking

Signposting
Phrases that tell the audience where they are in a talk. → Chapter 6


Word stress
The syllable pronounced with more force in a word (aNALysis). → Chapter 6


Elevator pitch
A 30-second summary of who you are and what you research. → Chapter 6


Clarification request
A phrase used to check you have understood a question. → Chapter 6


Linguistic inequality
The extra costs that the dominance of English imposes on non-native speakers in science. → Chapter 6
